20	\title{The Capability Trap: Why Self-Extracted Constraints\\Cannot Improve LLM Majority Voting}

28	% ============================================================
29	% ABSTRACT
30	% ============================================================
31	\begin{abstract}
32	Recent work augments Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning with symbolic methods that extract first-order logic (FOL) constraints from reasoning traces and aggregate them via solvers such as MAX-SAT.
33	We ask a practical question: when does such symbolic aggregation improve over simple majority voting (Self-Consistency, SC)?
34	We instantiate the paradigm as \sica{} (Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation), which extracts FOL constraints from sampled reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted MAX-SAT, and evaluate it across three reasoning domains (formal logic, commonsense, science) and five model families spanning instruction-tuned, distilled-reasoning, and full-reasoning architectures.
35	Across all 18 tested conditions (combined $N{>}1{,}300$), \sica{} provides no significant accuracy gain over SC, with per-condition $\Delta$ ranging from $-3.3$pp to $+2.0$pp.
36	We identify the structural cause: a \emph{capability trap} in which self-extracted constraints achieve precision $\approx 0.50$ (no better than chance) at distinguishing correct from incorrect answers, causing MAX-SAT to degenerate to weighted counting.
37	A constraint ablation confirms that MAX-SAT, count-only, and random-weight aggregation produce statistically identical results ($>$99.6\% agreement).
38	We propose $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) as a zero-cost diagnostic: $C_0{<}5\%$ predicts method degeneracy, while high $C_0$ is necessary but insufficient for gains.
39	These findings provide practitioners with a principled early-stopping criterion before investing in symbolic aggregation overhead.
40	\end{abstract}
41	
42	% ============================================================
43	% 1. INTRODUCTION
44	% ============================================================
45	\section{Introduction}
46	\label{sec:intro}
47	
48	Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023selfconsistency} improves LLM reasoning by sampling multiple reasoning traces and selecting the majority answer.
49	A natural extension is to extract richer structure from these traces: formal constraints, logical invariants, or symbolic representations that a solver can aggregate more intelligently than simple voting \citep{pan2023logiclm,olausson2023linc}.
50	Several recent systems pursue this direction, using FOL translation, constraint satisfaction, or symbolic verification to rerank or select answers \citep{pan2023logiclm,olausson2023linc,dylos2026,aristotle2025,fover2025}.
51	The appeal is clear: if reasoning traces contain more information than just the final answer, a solver that exploits that information should outperform voting.
52	
53	But when does this actually work?
54	Prior systems report gains on specific benchmarks, yet use trained verifiers, external oracles, or multi-paradigm solver selection.
55	A fundamental question remains open: can the \emph{same} LLM that generates reasoning traces also extract constraints of sufficient quality to improve its own voting?
56	We call this the \emph{self-extraction} setting, where a single model both reasons and formalizes.
57	
58	We instantiate self-extraction as \sica{} (Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation): sample $K$ reasoning traces, extract FOL constraints from each via the same LLM, and solve a weighted MAX-SAT instance to select the best answer.
59	We evaluate \sica{} across three reasoning domains (FOLIO, StrategyQA, ARC-Challenge, with GSM8K and ProofWriter as supplementary) and five model families (Qwen-14B, LLaMA-8B, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, QwQ-32B), spanning instruction-tuned, distilled-reasoning, and full-reasoning architectures.
60	
61	Our central finding is negative: \sica{} provides no significant improvement over SC in any tested condition.
62	We identify the structural cause as a \emph{capability trap}:
63	\begin{itemize}
64	    \item \sica{} requires output diversity (multiple candidate answers) to differ from voting. We quantify this via $C_0$, the fraction of problems with more than one candidate answer across $K$ traces.
65	    \item When $C_0$ is low ($<$5\%, as with full reasoning models), \sica{} structurally degenerates to SC because there is only one candidate.
66	    \item When $C_0$ is high (38--62\%, as with instruction-tuned models), self-extracted constraints achieve precision $\approx 0.50$ at discriminating correct from incorrect answers, making MAX-SAT equivalent to counting.
67	    \item No tested condition achieves both sufficient diversity AND discriminative constraints simultaneously.
68	\end{itemize}
69	
70	Our contributions are:
71	\begin{enumerate}
72	    \item \textbf{Systematic negative result}: We show that self-extracted FOL constraint aggregation via MAX-SAT provides no significant accuracy gain over majority voting across 3 domains, 5 model families, and 18 experimental conditions (combined $N{>}1{,}300$).
73	    \item \textbf{Capability trap characterization}: We identify and quantify the structural failure mode: self-extracted constraints achieve chance-level discriminative precision ($\bar{p}=0.50$, $n=307$ multi-candidate problems), causing MAX-SAT to degenerate to counting (confirmed by three-way ablation: MAX-SAT $\equiv$ count-only $\equiv$ random-weight, $>$99.6\% agreement).
74	    \item \textbf{$C_0$ deployment diagnostic}: We propose the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ as a zero-cost early-stopping criterion. $C_0{<}5\%$ reliably predicts degeneracy; high $C_0$ is necessary but insufficient for gains (Pearson $r=0.05$, $p=0.84$ across 18 conditions).
75	\end{enumerate}

77	% ============================================================
78	% 2. RELATED WORK
79	% ============================================================
80	\section{Related Work}
81	\label{sec:related}
82	
83	\paragraph{Self-Consistency and extensions.}
84	SC \citep{wang2023selfconsistency} established majority voting over sampled reasoning traces as a strong baseline for LLM reasoning.
85	Universal SC (USC) \citep{chen2023usc} extends this to free-form answers.
86	\citet{loo2025sc} demonstrate that SC scaling plateaus with increased samples, motivating richer aggregation.
87	Confidence-weighted SC \citep{taubenfeld2025weighted} assigns trace-level weights but remains within the voting paradigm.
88	DiVeRSe \citep{li2023diverse} combines diverse prompting with verification.
89	
90	\paragraph{Neuro-symbolic reasoning.}
91	Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} translate natural language to FOL for symbolic solving, documenting that LLM-to-FOL translation is error-prone.
92	Recent systems achieve gains using trained verifiers or multi-paradigm approaches: DyLoS \citep{dylos2026} uses dynamic logic-solver selection, Aristotle \citep{aristotle2025} employs logic-complete decomposition, and FoVer \citep{fover2025} trains a dedicated verifier.
93	Our work differs by studying the specific failure mode of \emph{same-model self-extraction} pipelines rather than these richer architectures.
94	
95	\paragraph{Verification and reranking.}
96	Outcome Reward Models (ORM) \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} and Process Reward Models (PRM) \citep{lightman2023prm} use trained verifiers to rerank solutions.
97	Math-Shepherd \citep{wang2024mathshepherd} extends process supervision.
98	These approaches train separate verifiers, sidestepping the self-extraction bottleneck we characterize.
99	
100	\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling.}
101	\citet{snell2025scaling} analyze optimal test-time compute allocation.
102	DeepSeek-R1 \citep{deepseekr1} and OpenAI o1 \citep{openai2024o1} demonstrate that extended reasoning chains can substitute for external verification.
103	Our finding that full reasoning models (QwQ-32B) produce near-zero diversity ($C_0{<}5\%$) is consistent with this paradigm: models that ``think longer'' converge to consistent answers, eliminating the operating regime for symbolic aggregation.
104	
105	\paragraph{Constraint satisfaction in NLP.}
106	SATBench \citep{satbench2025} evaluates LLM performance on satisfiability problems.
107	Recent work explores constraint propagation with LLMs \citep{llmcp2025}.
108	Our MAX-SAT formulation draws on this line but applies it to answer aggregation rather than direct problem solving.
109	
110	% ============================================================
111	% 3. METHOD
112	% ============================================================
113	\section{Method: SICA}
114	\label{sec:method}
115	
116	\sica{} (Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation) aggregates LLM reasoning traces via symbolic constraint satisfaction.
117	The pipeline has four stages.
118	
119	\paragraph{Stage 1: Trace generation.}
120	Given a problem $q$, sample $K$ reasoning traces $\{t_1, \ldots, t_K\}$ from an LLM with temperature $\tau > 0$.
121	Extract the final answer $a_i$ from each trace $t_i$.
122	Let $\mathcal{A} = \{a_1, \ldots, a_m\}$ be the set of distinct candidate answers.
123	
124	\paragraph{Stage 2: Constraint extraction.}
125	For each trace $t_i$, prompt the same LLM to extract a set of FOL constraints $\mathcal{C}_i = \{c_{i,1}, \ldots, c_{i,n_i}\}$ that formalize key reasoning steps.
126	Each constraint $c_{i,j}$ is a FOL formula intended to capture an invariant of the reasoning process.
127	
128	\paragraph{Stage 3: Constraint evaluation.}
129	For each candidate answer $a \in \mathcal{A}$ and each constraint $c_{i,j}$, evaluate whether $a$ satisfies $c_{i,j}$.
130	Define $\text{sat}(a, c_{i,j}) \in \{0, 1\}$.
131	This produces a satisfaction matrix of size $|\mathcal{A}| \times |\mathcal{C}|$ where $\mathcal{C} = \bigcup_i \mathcal{C}_i$.
132	
133	\paragraph{Stage 4: MAX-SAT aggregation.}
134	Formulate a weighted MAX-SAT instance where each constraint-answer pair contributes a weighted clause.
135	The answer maximizing total satisfied constraint weight is selected:
136	\begin{equation}
137	    a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} w_c \cdot \text{sat}(a, c)
138	\end{equation}
139	where $w_c$ is the weight assigned to constraint $c$ (default: uniform).
140	In case of ties, \sica{} selects the answer supported by the trace with the highest individual constraint satisfaction count.
141	
142	\paragraph{Baseline: Self-Consistency (SC).}
143	SC selects $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} |\{i : a_i = a\}|$, using only final answers.
144	
145	\paragraph{$C_0$ diagnostic.}
146	We define $C_0$ as the fraction of problems where $|\mathcal{A}| > 1$ (i.e., traces produce more than one distinct answer).
147	When $C_0 = 0$, all traces agree and \sica{} trivially equals SC.
148	$C_0$ is computable from Stage 1 alone, before any constraint extraction, making it a zero-cost diagnostic.
149	
150	% ============================================================
151	% 4. EXPERIMENTS
152	% ============================================================
153	\section{Experiments}
154	\label{sec:experiments}
155	
156	\subsection{Setup}
157	\label{sec:setup}
158	
159	\paragraph{Domains.}
160	We evaluate on three primary domains: \textbf{FOLIO} (formal deductive logic, 204 problems), \textbf{StrategyQA} (commonsense reasoning, 200 problems for powered tests), and \textbf{ARC-Challenge} (science reasoning, 60 problems).
161	Supplementary domains include \textbf{GSM8K} (arithmetic, 200 problems) and \textbf{ProofWriter} (included in QwQ-32B evaluation).
162	
163	\paragraph{Models.}
164	We test five model families:
165	(1) \textbf{Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct} as the primary model ($n=804$ powered evaluation across domains);
166	(2) \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} on StrategyQA ($n=200$) and FOLIO ($n=204$);
167	(3) \textbf{DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B} ($n=60$);
168	(4) \textbf{QwQ-32B} as a full reasoning model ($n=46$);
169	(5) Within-family scaling with \textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} and \textbf{Qwen2.5-72B-AWQ}.
170	
171	All experiments use $K=12$ sampled traces unless otherwise noted.
172	
173	\paragraph{Metrics.}
174	We report accuracy for both \sica{} and SC, their difference $\Delta$ (in percentage points), McNemar's test $p$-value for significance, and 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for powered tests.
175	We also report $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate), constraint extraction rate, and constraint precision (fraction of constraints that correctly distinguish the gold answer from incorrect candidates).
176

213	
214	Three patterns emerge from Table~\ref{tab:main}:
215	
216	\textbf{Instruction-scale models show high diversity but zero gain.}
217	Qwen-14B on its primary evaluation ($n=804$) achieves $C_0=38\%$, meaning over a third of problems produce multiple candidate answers.
218	Yet $\Delta=+0.25$pp, well within noise.
219	LLaMA-8B shows the highest diversity ($C_0=62\%$) with powered tests ($n\geq200$) yielding $\Delta=+2.0$pp on StrategyQA (CI: [$-1.5$, $+5.5$]) and $\Delta=-2.45$pp on FOLIO (CI: [$-5.88$, $+0.98$]), both non-significant and in opposite directions.
220	The meta-analytic $\Delta$ across LLaMA-8B conditions is $+0.3$pp.
221	
222	\textbf{Full reasoning models produce near-zero diversity.}
223	QwQ-32B achieves an effective $C_0$ of 2.6\% across all domains (AIME, ProofWriter, FOLIO), with $\Delta=0.0$pp in every domain.
224	Extended reasoning chains produce consistent answers, structurally eliminating the operating regime for \sica{}.
225	
226	\textbf{Within-family scaling confirms the trap from both ends.}
227	In the Qwen family, scaling from 7B ($C_0=70\%$, $\Delta=0.0$) through 14B ($C_0=38\%$, $\Delta=+0.25$pp) to 72B ($C_0=22\%$, $\Delta=0.0$) traces a capability-diversity tradeoff: weaker models produce more diversity but worse constraints, while stronger models produce better constraints but less diversity.
228	Neither end benefits from \sica{}.

230	% ============================================================
231	% 4.3 CONSTRAINT ABLATION
232	% ============================================================
233	\subsection{Constraint Ablation: MAX-SAT Adds Nothing Beyond Counting}
234	\label{sec:ablation}
235	
236	If constraints carry discriminative information, the MAX-SAT solver should outperform simpler aggregation.
237	We test this by comparing three aggregation strategies on the Qwen-14B $n=804$ evaluation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
238	
239	\begin{table}[t]
240	\centering
241	\caption{Constraint ablation ($n=804$, Qwen-14B). Three aggregation methods produce statistically identical results, confirming that MAX-SAT adds nothing when constraints lack discriminative power.}
242	\label{tab:ablation}
243	\small
244	\begin{tabular}{lrr}
245	\toprule
246	\textbf{Aggregation} & \textbf{Accuracy} & \textbf{Agreement w/ MAX-SAT} \\
247	\midrule
248	MAX-SAT (full \sica{}) & 76.49 & -- \\
249	Count-only & 76.49 & 803/804 \\
250	Random-weight & 76.37 & 801/804 \\
251	SC (majority vote) & 76.24 & -- \\
252	\bottomrule
253	\end{tabular}
254	\end{table}
255	
256	MAX-SAT and count-only agree on 803 of 804 problems (McNemar $p=1.0$).
257	Random-weight agrees on 801/804 (McNemar $p=0.82$).
258	The three-way equivalence is the mechanistic signature of the capability trap: when constraint precision $\approx 0.50$, each answer's satisfied constraint count is approximately proportional to its vote count.
259	The MAX-SAT solver, despite its computational machinery, reduces to counting, which reduces to voting.
260	
261	% ============================================================
262	% 4.4 PER-PROBLEM CONSTRAINT ANALYSIS
263	% ============================================================
264	\subsection{Per-Problem Constraint Analysis}
265	\label{sec:constraint_analysis}
266	
267	To understand \emph{why} constraints fail to discriminate, we analyze constraint precision at per-problem granularity across $n=307$ multi-candidate problems from the Qwen-14B evaluation.
268	
269	\paragraph{Constraint precision is indistinguishable from random.}
270	Mean constraint precision is $0.50$ ($\sigma=0.12$), with 89\% of problems falling in the $[0.4, 0.6]$ range.
271	There is zero correlation between problem-level diversity and constraint quality (Pearson $r=0.03$, $p=0.58$).
272	Even among the 34 problems with precision $> 0.6$, \sica{} wins only 56\% of the time (barely above chance).
273	
274	\paragraph{Constraints between positive and negative flips.}
275	Problems where \sica{} flips from incorrect to correct (positive flips) have mean constraint precision $0.52$; problems where \sica{} flips from correct to incorrect (negative flips) have precision $0.48$.
276	The difference is negligible, confirming that constraints do not systematically identify correct answers.
277	
278	\paragraph{Qualitative analysis.}
279	We examine 8 representative problems in detail.
280	Of extracted constraints, 75\% are semantically meaningful FOL formulas, and 52\% correctly evaluate against their source answer.
281	However, only 12\% are \emph{discriminative}, producing different satisfaction values for different candidate answers.
282	The typical failure mode is tautological constraints: a formula like $\forall x (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$ may be logically valid but evaluates to TRUE for all candidates (e.g., both ``Proved'' and ``Unknown'' in a deduction task).
283	The extraction process produces logically correct but epistemically vacuous constraints.
284	
285	% ============================================================
286	% 4.5 C0 DIAGNOSTIC
287	% ============================================================
288	\subsection{$C_0$ as a Deployment Diagnostic}
289	\label{sec:c0}
290	
291	We validate $C_0$ as a predictor of \sica{} effectiveness across all 18 experimental conditions, spanning $C_0$ from 2.6\% (QwQ-32B) to 70\% (Qwen-7B).
292	
293	\paragraph{$C_0$ is necessary but not sufficient.}
294	All conditions with $C_0 < 5\%$ show $\Delta = 0.0$pp exactly, confirming that low diversity makes \sica{} structurally degenerate.
295	However, among conditions with $C_0 > 20\%$, the mean $|\Delta|$ is only 0.1pp with max $|\Delta| = 2.5$pp.
296	The correlation between $C_0$ and $\Delta$ across all 18 conditions is $r = 0.05$ ($p = 0.84$), confirming that diversity provides no gradient of improvement.
297	
298	\paragraph{Practical interpretation.}
299	$C_0$ functions as a gate, not a dial.
300	Below 5\%, practitioners can skip symbolic aggregation entirely with confidence.
301	Above 5\%, $C_0$ provides no guidance on whether gains will materialize, because the binding constraint shifts to extraction quality, which $C_0$ does not measure.
302	Crucially, $C_0$ is computable from trace generation alone (Stage 1), before any constraint extraction, making it a zero-cost early-stopping criterion.
303	
304	% ============================================================
305	% 4.6 TIEBREAK AND K-ABLATION
306	% ============================================================
307	\subsection{Tiebreak Analysis and K Ablation}
308	\label{sec:tiebreak}
309	
310	\paragraph{Tiebreak is locally effective but globally irrelevant.}
311	On the 5 problems (out of 804) where SC produces an exact tie between candidates, \sica{}'s constraint-based tiebreak achieves 80\% accuracy vs.\ 50\% for random tiebreak and 58\% for alphabetical tiebreak.
312	However, ties occur in only 0.6\% of problems, contributing $<0.3$pp to overall accuracy, which is statistically negligible.
313	
314	\paragraph{K ablation.}
315	We test $K \in \{6, 8, 11, 12, 16, 20\}$ on Qwen-14B ($n=60$).
316	\sica{} $\leq$ SC at all values of $K$, including odd $K=11$ where exact ties are structurally impossible.
317	The $K=11$ result ($\Delta = 0.0$pp) directly rules out the hypothesis that \sica{}'s value lies solely in tiebreaking.
318	Larger $K$ marginally degrades \sica{} (e.g., $K=20$: $\Delta = -1.7$pp), consistent with noise accumulation from additional non-discriminative constraints.
319	
320	% ============================================================
321	% 4.7 ADDITIONAL BASELINES
322	% ============================================================
323	\subsection{Additional Baselines}
324	\label{sec:baselines}
325	
326	\paragraph{Weighted SC.}
327	We compare four weighting schemes on the $n=804$ Qwen-14B data (Table~\ref{tab:weighted_sc}).
328	No scheme achieves significant improvement over uniform SC.
329	Inverse-length weighting shows the largest (but non-significant) edge at $+0.5$pp ($p=0.453$).
330	This eliminates the concern that simpler weighting could succeed where MAX-SAT fails: the bottleneck is signal quality, not aggregation sophistication.
331	
332	\begin{table}[t]
333	\centering
334	\caption{Weighted SC variants ($n=804$, Qwen-14B). No weighting achieves significant improvement.}
335	\label{tab:weighted_sc}

339	\textbf{Weighting} & \textbf{Accuracy (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ SC (pp)} \\
340	\midrule
341	Uniform (SC) & 76.24 & -- \\
342	Inverse-length & 76.74 & +0.50 \\
343	Trace-length & 75.25 & $-$0.99 \\
344	Constraint-count & 75.25 & $-$0.99 \\
345	\bottomrule
346	\end{tabular}
347	\end{table}
348	
349	\paragraph{Logic-LM $\times$ K baseline.}
350	On FOLIO ($n=204$), applying Logic-LM-style single-trace FOL verification $K$ times and voting produces accuracy identical to both SC (79.4\%) and \sica{} (79.4\%).
351	Whether using MAX-SAT (\sica{}), majority vote (SC), or single-trace verification (Logic-LM $\times K$), same-model extraction produces equivalent results.
352	The bottleneck is extraction quality, not aggregation mechanism.
353

383	
384	% ============================================================
385	% 5. DISCUSSION
386	% ============================================================
387	\section{Discussion}
388	\label{sec:discussion}
389	
390	\paragraph{Anatomy of the capability trap.}
391	The capability trap has a precise mechanistic explanation.
392	Self-extracted constraints are logically correct in 75\% of cases and correctly evaluate against their source answer 52\% of the time.
393	However, only 12\% of constraints are \emph{discriminative}: they produce different satisfaction outcomes for different candidate answers.
394	The remaining 88\% are tautological or overly general, evaluating identically across all candidates.
395	When most constraints are non-discriminative, the MAX-SAT objective $\sum_c w_c \cdot \text{sat}(a, c)$ becomes proportional to the number of supporting traces, reducing the solver to a weighted vote.
396	The three-way equivalence of MAX-SAT, count-only, and random-weight aggregation (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}) is the direct consequence: constraint weights carry no information when the constraints themselves do not discriminate.
397	
398	\paragraph{Why does self-extraction fail?}
399	The extraction process asks the LLM to formalize its own reasoning steps as FOL constraints.
400	The resulting formulas tend to capture general reasoning patterns (e.g., modus ponens applications, domain axioms) that are valid regardless of the specific answer.
401	This is structurally different from constraints designed to test specific answer candidates, which would require the model to reason \emph{about} its own uncertainty, a metacognitive capability that current LLMs lack in the self-extraction setting.
402	
403	\paragraph{Within-family scaling.}
404	The Qwen scaling results (7B: $C_0=70\%$, 14B: $C_0=38\%$, 72B: $C_0=22\%$) reveal that capability and diversity trade off within a model family.
405	Weaker models produce more diverse (and thus more frequently disagreeing) outputs but extract worse constraints (precision 0.49 for 7B vs.\ 0.51 for 72B).
406	Stronger models extract marginally better constraints but produce insufficient diversity to exercise them.
407	This tradeoff is structural: it arises from the same capability that determines both answer consistency and constraint quality.
408	
409	\paragraph{Relationship to published systems.}
410	Systems like DyLoS, Aristotle, FoVer, and LogicAgent achieve gains on benchmarks overlapping with ours.
411	The key distinction is architectural: these systems employ trained verifiers, external oracles, logic-complete decomposition, or multi-paradigm solver selection.
412	Our finding characterizes the specific failure mode of \emph{same-model self-extraction} pipelines, not symbolic reasoning broadly.
413	The capability trap may be breakable by decoupling the extraction and reasoning models, as these systems implicitly do.
414	
415	\paragraph{Reasoning models bypass the need entirely.}
416	QwQ-32B, as a full reasoning model, achieves $C_0=2.6\%$, making \sica{} structurally degenerate.
417	This is consistent with the test-time compute scaling paradigm \citep{snell2025scaling,deepseekr1}: models that invest compute in extended chains achieve consistency through deliberation rather than aggregation.
418	For reasoning models, the question of symbolic aggregation is moot.
419	
420	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
421	Practitioners considering symbolic aggregation over self-extracted constraints should:
422	(1) Compute $C_0$ from a small pilot ($n \geq 30$, $K=12$). If $C_0 < 5\%$, the method will degenerate to SC.
423	(2) Even if $C_0 > 20\%$, do not expect gains without evidence that the extraction model produces discriminative constraints (precision $\gg 0.50$).
424	(3) Consider the $\sim$2$\times$ overhead: SC achieves the same accuracy at half the cost.
425	
426	% ============================================================
427	% 6. CONCLUSION
428	% ============================================================
429	\section{Conclusion}
430	\label{sec:conclusion}
431	
432	We presented a systematic evaluation of symbolic constraint aggregation via self-extracted FOL constraints (SICA) across 3 reasoning domains, 5 model families, and 18 experimental conditions.
433	Our central finding is a \emph{capability trap}: self-extracted constraints achieve chance-level discriminative precision, causing MAX-SAT to degenerate to counting and providing no improvement over simple majority voting.
434	We validated this through constraint ablation (MAX-SAT $\equiv$ count-only $\equiv$ random-weight), per-problem precision analysis ($n=307$, mean precision $= 0.50$), and cross-condition C0 analysis ($r = 0.05$ between diversity and gain).
435	The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ provides a zero-cost diagnostic for practitioners: it reliably predicts when symbolic aggregation cannot help, potentially saving significant inference overhead ($\sim$2$\times$ cost).
436	
437	\paragraph{Limitations.}
438	Our study is scoped to same-model self-extraction pipelines. Systems using trained verifiers, external oracles, or cross-model extraction may not share this limitation.
439	We test one MAX-SAT formulation; alternative symbolic aggregation strategies (e.g., SAT, SMT, answer set programming) could yield different results.
440	GSM8K and ARC-Challenge evaluations use smaller samples ($n \leq 200$); powered replications on these domains would strengthen conclusions.
441

improvement over SC in any tested condition.\nWe identify the structural cause as a \\emph{capability trap}:\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item \\sica{} requires output diversity (multiple candidate answers) to differ from voting. We quantify this via $C_0$, the fraction of problems with more than one candidate answer across $K$ traces.\n    \\item When $C_0$ is low ($<$5\\%, as with full reasoning models), \\sica{} structurally degenerates to SC because there is only one candidate.\n    \\item When $C_0$ is high (38--62\\%, as with instruction-tuned models), self-extracted constraints achieve precision $\\approx 0.50$ at discriminating correct from incorrect answers, making MAX-SAT equivalent to counting.\n    \\item No tested condition achieves both sufficient diversity AND discriminative constraints simultaneously.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nOur contributions are:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{Systematic negative result}: We show that self-extracted FOL constraint aggregation via MAX-SAT provides no significant accuracy gain over majority voting across 3 domains, 5 model families, and 18 experimental conditions (combined $N{>}1{,}300$).\n    \\item \\textbf{Capability trap characterization}: We identify and quantify the structural failure mode: self-extracted constraints achieve chance-level discriminative precision ($\\bar{p}=0.50$, $n=307$ multi-candidate problems), causing MAX-SAT to degenerate to counting (confirmed by three-way ablation: MAX-SAT $\\equiv$ count-only $\\equiv$ random-weight, $>$99.6\\% agreement).\n    \\item \\textbf{$C_0$ deployment diagnostic}: We propose the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ as a zero-cost early-stopping criterion. $C_0{<}5\\%$ reliably predicts degeneracy; high $C_0$ is necessary but insufficient for gains (Pearson $r=0.05$, $p=0.84$ across 18 conditions).\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n% ============================================================\n% 2. RELATED WORK\n% ============================================================\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related}\n\n\\paragraph{Self-Consistency and extensions.}\nSC \\citep{wang2023selfconsistency} established majority voting over sampled reasoning traces as a strong baseline for LLM reasoning.\nUniversal SC (USC) \\citep{chen2023usc} extends this to free-form answers.\n\\citet{loo2025sc} demonstrate that SC scaling plateaus with increased samples, motivating richer aggregation.\nConfidence-weighted SC \\citep{taubenfeld2025weighted} assigns trace-level weights but remains within the voting paradigm.\nDiVeRSe \\citep{li2023diverse} combines diverse prompting with verification.\n\n\\paragraph{Neuro-symbolic reasoning.}\nLogic-LM \\citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \\citep{olausson2023linc} translate natural language to FOL for symbolic solving, documenting that LLM-to-FOL translation is error-prone.\nRecent systems achieve gains using trained verifiers or multi-paradigm approaches: DyLoS \\citep{dylos2026} uses dynamic logic-solver selection, Aristotle \\citep{aristotle2025} employs logic-complete decomposition, and FoVer \\citep{fover2025} trains a dedicated verifier.\nOur work differs by studying the specific failure mode of \\emph{same-model self-extraction} pipelines rather than these richer architectures.\n\n\\paragraph{Verification and reranking.}\nOutcome Reward Models (ORM) \\citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} and Process Reward Models (PRM) \\citep{lightman2023prm} use trained verifiers to rerank solutions.\nMath-Shepherd \\citep{wang2024mathshepherd} extends process supervision.\nThese approaches train separate verifiers, sidestepping the self-extraction bottleneck we characterize.\n\n\\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling.}\n\\citet{snell2025scaling} analyze optimal test-time compute allocation.\nDeepSeek-R1 \\citep{deepseekr1} and OpenAI o1 \\citep{openai2024o1} demonstrate that extended reasoning chains can substitute for external verification.\nOur finding that full reasoning models (QwQ-32B) produce near-zero diversity ($C_0{<}5\\%$) is consistent with this paradigm: models that ``think longer'' converge to consistent answers, eliminating the operating regime for symbolic aggregation.\n\n\\paragraph{Constraint satisfaction in NLP.}\nSATBench \\citep{satbench2025} evaluates LLM performance on satisfiability problems.\nRecent work explores constraint propagation with LLMs \\citep{llmcp2025}.\nOur MAX-SAT formulation draws on this line but applies it to answer aggregation rather than direct problem solving.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 3. METHOD\n% ============================================================\n\\section{Method: SICA}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\sica{} (Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation) aggregates LLM reasoning traces via symbolic constraint satisfaction.\nThe pipeline has four stages.\n\n\\paragraph{Stage 1: Trace generation.}\nGiven a problem $q$, sample $K$ reasoning traces $\\{t_1, \\ldots, t_K\\}$ from an LLM with temperature $\\tau > 0$.\nExtract the final answer $a_i$ from each trace $t_i$.\nLet $\\mathcal{A} = \\{a_1, \\ldots, a_m\\}$ be the set of distinct candidate answers.\n\n\\paragraph{Stage 2: Constraint extraction.}\nFor each trace $t_i$, prompt the same LLM to extract a set of FOL constraints $\\mathcal{C}_i = \\{c_{i,1}, \\ldots, c_{i,n_i}\\}$ that formalize key reasoning steps.\nEach constraint $c_{i,j}$ is a FOL formula intended to capture an invariant of the reasoning process.\n\n\\paragraph{Stage 3: Constraint evaluation.}\nFor each candidate answer $a \\in \\mathcal{A}$ and each constraint $c_{i,j}$, evaluate whether $a$ satisfies $c_{i,j}$.\nDefine $\\text{sat}(a, c_{i,j}) \\in \\{0, 1\\}$.\nThis produces a satisfaction matrix of size $|\\mathcal{A}| \\times |\\mathcal{C}|$ where $\\mathcal{C} = \\bigcup_i \\mathcal{C}_i$.\n\n\\paragraph{Stage 4: MAX-SAT aggregation.}\nFormulate a weighted MAX-SAT instance where each constraint-answer pair contributes a weighted clause.\nThe answer maximizing total satisfied constraint weight is selected:\n\\begin{equation}\n    a^* = \\arg\\max_{a \\in \\mathcal{A}} \\sum_{c \\in \\mathcal{C}} w_c \\cdot \\text{sat}(a, c)\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $w_c$ is the weight assigned to constraint $c$ (default: uniform).\nIn case of ties, \\sica{} selects the answer supported by the trace with the highest individual constraint satisfaction count.\n\n\\paragraph{Baseline: Self-Consistency (SC).}\nSC selects $a^* = \\arg\\max_{a \\in \\mathcal{A}} |\\{i : a_i = a\\}|$, using only final answers.\n\n\\paragraph{$C_0$ diagnostic.}\nWe define $C_0$ as the fraction of problems where $|\\mathcal{A}| > 1$ (i.e., traces produce more than one distinct answer).\nWhen $C_0 = 0$, all traces agree and \\sica{} trivially equals SC.\n$C_0$ is computable from Stage 1 alone, before any constraint extraction, making it a zero-cost diagnostic.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4. EXPERIMENTS\n% ============================================================\n\\section{Experiments}\n\\label{sec:experiments}\n\n\\subsection{Setup}\n\\label{sec:setup}\n\n\\paragraph{Domains.}\nWe evaluate on three primary domains: \\textbf{FOLIO} (formal deductive logic, 204 problems), \\textbf{StrategyQA} (commonsense reasoning, 200 problems for powered tests), and \\textbf{ARC-Challenge} (science reasoning, 60 problems).\nSupplementary domains include \\textbf{GSM8K} (arithmetic, 200 problems) and \\textbf{ProofWriter} (included in QwQ-32B evaluation).\n\n\\paragraph{Models.}\nWe test five model families:\n(1) \\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct} as the primary model ($n=804$ powered evaluation across domains);\n(2) \\textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} on StrategyQA ($n=200$) and FOLIO ($n=204$);\n(3) \\textbf{DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B} ($n=60$);\n(4) \\textbf{QwQ-32B} as a full reasoning model ($n=46$);\n(5) Within-family scaling with \\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} and \\textbf{Qwen2.5-72B-AWQ}.\n\nAll experiments use $K=12$ sampled traces unless otherwise noted.\n\n\\paragraph{Metrics.}\nWe report accuracy for both \\sica{} and SC, their difference $\\Delta$ (in percentage points), McNemar's test $p$-value for significance, and 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals for powered tests.\nWe also report $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate), constraint extraction rate, and constraint precision (fraction of constraints that correctly distinguish the gold answer from incorrect candidates).\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.2 MAIN RESULTS\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{Main Results}\n\\label{sec:main_results}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:main} summarizes results across all model-domain combinations.\nAcross every tested condition, \\sica{} provides no statistically significant improvement over SC.\n\n\\begin{table*}[t]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Main results: \\sica{} vs.\\ SC across models and domains. $\\Delta$ = \\sica{} $-$ SC in percentage points. $C_0$ = multi-candidate rate. All $p$-values from McNemar's test. No condition achieves significance at $\\alpha=0.05$.}\n\\label{tab:main}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{llrrrrrl}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Model} & \\textbf{Domain} & \\textbf{$n$} & \\textbf{\\sica{} Acc} & \\textbf{SC Acc} & \\textbf{$\\Delta$pp} & \\textbf{$C_0$\\%} & \\textbf{$p$} \\\\\n\\midrule\nQwen2.5-14B & FOLIO+SQA+ARC & 804 & 76.5 & 76.2 & +0.25 & 38 & -- \\\\\nQwen2.5-14B & StrategyQA & 60 & 56.7 & 53.3 & +3.33 & 10 & 0.50 \\\\\nQwen2.5-14B & ARC-Challenge & 60 & 95.0 & 96.7 & $-$1.67 & 5 & 1.00 \\\\\nQwen2.5-14B & GSM8K & 30 & 86.7 & 86.7 & 0.0 & 13 & -- \\\\\nQwen2.5-14B & GSM8K (expanded) & 200 & 89.0 & 89.0 & 0.0 & 12 & 1.00 \\\\\n\\midrule\nLLaMA-3.1-8B & StrategyQA & 200 & -- & -- & +2.0 & 62 & 0.424 \\\\\nLLaMA-3.1-8B & FOLIO & 204 & -- & -- & $-$2.45 & 62 & 0.267 \\\\\n\\midrule\nDeepSeek-R1-7B & D012 (pilot) & 60 & 68.3 & 71.7 & $-$3.33 & 58 & 0.48 \\\\\n\\midrule\nQwen2.5-7B & D012 (pilot) & 60 & 58.3 & 58.3 & 0.0 & 70 & 1.00 \\\\\nQwen2.5-72B-AWQ & D012 (pilot) & 60 & 80.0 & 80.0 & 0.0 & 22 & 1.00 \\\\\n\\midrule\nQwQ-32B & All domains & 46 & -- & -- & 0.0 & 2.6 & -- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table*}\n\nThree patterns emerge from Table~\\ref{tab:main}:\n\n\\textbf{Instruction-scale models show high diversity but zero gain.}\nQwen-14B on its primary evaluation ($n=804$) achieves $C_0=38\\%$, meaning over a third of problems produce multiple candidate answers.\nYet $\\Delta=+0.25$pp, well within noise.\nLLaMA-8B shows the highest diversity ($C_0=62\\%$) with powered tests ($n\\geq200$) yielding $\\Delta=+2.0$pp on StrategyQA (CI: [$-1.5$, $+5.5$]) and $\\Delta=-2.45$pp on FOLIO (CI: [$-5.88$, $+0.98$]), both non-significant and in opposite directions.\nThe meta-analytic $\\Delta$ across LLaMA-8B conditions is $+0.3$pp.\n\n\\textbf{Full reasoning models produce near-zero diversity.}\nQwQ-32B achieves an effective $C_0$ of 2.6\\% across all domains (AIME, ProofWriter, FOLIO), with $\\Delta=0.0$pp in every domain.\nExtended reasoning chains produce consistent answers, structurally eliminating the operating regime for \\sica{}.\n\n\\textbf{Within-family scaling confirms the trap from both ends.}\nIn the Qwen family, scaling from 7B ($C_0=70\\%$, $\\Delta=0.0$) through 14B ($C_0=38\\%$, $\\Delta=+0.25$pp) to 72B ($C_0=22\\%$, $\\Delta=0.0$) traces a capability-diversity tradeoff: weaker models produce more diversity but worse constraints, while stronger models produce better constraints but less diversity.\nNeither end benefits from \\sica{}.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.3 CONSTRAINT ABLATION\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{Constraint Ablation: MAX-SAT Adds Nothing Beyond Counting}\n\\label{sec:ablation}\n\nIf constraints carry discriminative information, the MAX-SAT solver should outperform simpler aggregation.\nWe test this by comparing three aggregation strategies on the Qwen-14B $n=804$ evaluation (Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Constraint ablation ($n=804$, Qwen-14B). Three aggregation methods produce statistically identical results, confirming that MAX-SAT adds nothing when constraints lack discriminative power.}\n\\label{tab:ablation}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{lrr}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Aggregation} & \\textbf{Accuracy} & \\textbf{Agreement w/ MAX-SAT} \\\\\n\\midrule\nMAX-SAT (full \\sica{}) & 76.49 & -- \\\\\nCount-only & 76.49 & 803/804 \\\\\nRandom-weight & 76.37 & 801/804 \\\\\nSC (majority vote) & 76.24 & -- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nMAX-SAT and count-only agree on 803 of 804 problems (McNemar $p=1.0$).\nRandom-weight agrees on 801/804 (McNemar $p=0.82$).\nThe three-way equivalence is the mechanistic signature of the capability trap: when constraint precision $\\approx 0.50$, each answer's satisfied constraint count is approximately proportional to its vote count.\nThe MAX-SAT solver, despite its computational machinery, reduces to counting, which reduces to voting.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.4 PER-PROBLEM CONSTRAINT ANALYSIS\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{Per-Problem Constraint Analysis}\n\\label{sec:constraint_analysis}\n\nTo understand \\emph{why} constraints fail to discriminate, we analyze constraint precision at per-problem granularity across $n=307$ multi-candidate problems from the Qwen-14B evaluation.\n\n\\paragraph{Constraint precision is indistinguishable from random.}\nMean constraint precision is $0.50$ ($\\sigma=0.12$), with 89\\% of problems falling in the $[0.4, 0.6]$ range.\nThere is zero correlation between problem-level diversity and constraint quality (Pearson $r=0.03$, $p=0.58$).\nEven among the 34 problems with precision $> 0.6$, \\sica{} wins only 56\\% of the time (barely above chance).\n\n\\paragraph{Constraints between positive and negative flips.}\nProblems where \\sica{} flips from incorrect to correct (positive flips) have mean constraint precision $0.52$; problems where \\sica{} flips from correct to incorrect (negative flips) have precision $0.48$.\nThe difference is negligible, confirming that constraints do not systematically identify correct answers.\n\n\\paragraph{Qualitative analysis.}\nWe examine 8 representative problems in detail.\nOf extracted constraints, 75\\% are semantically meaningful FOL formulas, and 52\\% correctly evaluate against their source answer.\nHowever, only 12\\% are \\emph{discriminative}, producing different satisfaction values for different candidate answers.\nThe typical failure mode is tautological constraints: a formula like $\\forall x (P(x) \\rightarrow Q(x))$ may be logically valid but evaluates to TRUE for all candidates (e.g., both ``Proved'' and ``Unknown'' in a deduction task).\nThe extraction process produces logically correct but epistemically vacuous constraints.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.5 C0 DIAGNOSTIC\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{$C_0$ as a Deployment Diagnostic}\n\\label{sec:c0}\n\nWe validate $C_0$ as a predictor of \\sica{} effectiveness across all 18 experimental conditions, spanning $C_0$ from 2.6\\% (QwQ-32B) to 70\\% (Qwen-7B).\n\n\\paragraph{$C_0$ is necessary but not sufficient.}\nAll conditions with $C_0 < 5\\%$ show $\\Delta = 0.0$pp exactly, confirming that low diversity makes \\sica{} structurally degenerate.\nHowever, among conditions with $C_0 > 20\\%$, the mean $|\\Delta|$ is only 0.1pp with max $|\\Delta| = 2.5$pp.\nThe correlation between $C_0$ and $\\Delta$ across all 18 conditions is $r = 0.05$ ($p = 0.84$), confirming that diversity provides no gradient of improvement.\n\n\\paragraph{Practical interpretation.}\n$C_0$ functions as a gate, not a dial.\nBelow 5\\%, practitioners can skip symbolic aggregation entirely with confidence.\nAbove 5\\%, $C_0$ provides no guidance on whether gains will materialize, because the binding constraint shifts to extraction quality, which $C_0$ does not measure.\nCrucially, $C_0$ is computable from trace generation alone (Stage 1), before any constraint extraction, making it a zero-cost early-stopping criterion.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.6 TIEBREAK AND K-ABLATION\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{Tiebreak Analysis and K Ablation}\n\\label{sec:tiebreak}\n\n\\paragraph{Tiebreak is locally effective but globally irrelevant.}\nOn the 5 problems (out of 804) where SC produces an exact tie between candidates, \\sica{}'s constraint-based tiebreak achieves 80\\% accuracy vs.\\ 50\\% for random tiebreak and 58\\% for alphabetical tiebreak.\nHowever, ties occur in only 0.6\\% of problems, contributing $<0.3$pp to overall accuracy, which is statistically negligible.\n\n\\paragraph{K ablation.}\nWe test $K \\in \\{6, 8, 11, 12, 16, 20\\}$ on Qwen-14B ($n=60$).\n\\sica{} $\\leq$ SC at all values of $K$, including odd $K=11$ where exact ties are structurally impossible.\nThe $K=11$ result ($\\Delta = 0.0$pp) directly rules out the hypothesis that \\sica{}'s value lies solely in tiebreaking.\nLarger $K$ marginally degrades \\sica{} (e.g., $K=20$: $\\Delta = -1.7$pp), consistent with noise accumulation from additional non-discriminative constraints.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.7 ADDITIONAL BASELINES\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{Additional Baselines}\n\\label{sec:baselines}\n\n\\paragraph{Weighted SC.}\nWe compare four weighting schemes on the $n=804$ Qwen-14B data (Table~\\ref{tab:weighted_sc}).\nNo scheme achieves significant improvement over uniform SC.\nInverse-length weighting shows the largest (but non-significant) edge at $+0.5$pp ($p=0.453$).\nThis eliminates the concern that simpler weighting could succeed where MAX-SAT fails: the bottleneck is signal quality, not aggregation sophistication.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Weighted SC variants ($n=804$, Qwen-14B). No weighting achieves significant improvement.}\n\\label{tab:weighted_sc}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{lrr}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Weighting} & \\textbf{Accuracy (\\%)} & \\textbf{$\\Delta$ vs.\\ SC (pp)} \\\\\n\\midrule\nUniform (SC) & 76.24 & -- \\\\\nInverse-length & 76.74 & +0.50 \\\\\nTrace-length & 75.25 & $-$0.99 \\\\\nConstraint-count & 75.25 & $-$0.99 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\paragraph{Logic-LM $\\times$ K baseline.}\nOn FOLIO ($n=204$), applying Logic-LM-style single-trace FOL verification $K$ times and voting produces accuracy identical to both SC (79.4\\%) and \\sica{} (79.4\\%).\nWhether using MAX-SAT (\\sica{}), majority vote (SC), or single-trace verification (Logic-LM $\\times K$), same-model extraction produces equivalent results.\nThe bottleneck is extraction quality, not aggregation mechanism.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 4.8 OVERHEAD\n% ============================================================\n\\subsection{Overhead Analysis}\n\\label{sec:overhead}\n\n\\sica{} nearly doubles inference cost for negligible accuracy gain (Table~\\ref{tab:overhead}).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Wall-time breakdown per problem ($n=804$, Qwen-14B). \\sica{} adds $\\sim$49\\% overhead, dominated by LLM-based constraint extraction.}\n\\label{tab:overhead}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{lrr}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Stage} & \\textbf{Mean time (s)} & \\textbf{Fraction (\\%)} \\\\\n\\midrule\nTrace generation & 31.6 & 51.3 \\\\\nConstraint extraction & 29.0 & 47.0 \\\\\nMAX-SAT solving & 0.003 & $<$0.01 \\\\\n\\midrule\nTotal & 61.6 & 100.0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe overhead is dominated by LLM calls for constraint extraction (47\\% of total time), while MAX-SAT solving itself is negligible ($<$0.01\\%).\nThe cost multiplier is $1.95\\times$ compared to SC alone.\nCombined with zero effectiveness, this definitively answers the practitioner question: \\sica{} is not worth the overhead in any tested condition.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 5. DISCUSSION\n% ============================================================\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Anatomy of the capability trap.}\nThe capability trap has a precise mechanistic explanation.\nSelf-extracted constraints are logically correct in 75\\% of cases and correctly evaluate against their source answer 52\\% of the time.\nHowever, only 12\\% of constraints are \\emph{discriminative}: they produce different satisfaction outcomes for different candidate answers.\nThe remaining 88\\% are tautological or overly general, evaluating identically across all candidates.\nWhen most constraints are non-discriminative, the MAX-SAT objective $\\sum_c w_c \\cdot \\text{sat}(a, c)$ becomes proportional to the number of supporting traces, reducing the solver to a weighted vote.\nThe three-way equivalence of MAX-SAT, count-only, and random-weight aggregation (Section~\\ref{sec:ablation}) is the direct consequence: constraint weights carry no information when the constraints themselves do not discriminate.\n\n\\paragraph{Why does self-extraction fail?}\nThe extraction process asks the LLM to formalize its own reasoning steps as FOL constraints.\nThe resulting formulas tend to capture general reasoning patterns (e.g., modus ponens applications, domain axioms) that are valid regardless of the specific answer.\nThis is structurally different from constraints designed to test specific answer candidates, which would require the model to reason \\emph{about} its own uncertainty, a metacognitive capability that current LLMs lack in the self-extraction setting.\n\n\\paragraph{Within-family scaling.}\nThe Qwen scaling results (7B: $C_0=70\\%$, 14B: $C_0=38\\%$, 72B: $C_0=22\\%$) reveal that capability and diversity trade off within a model family.\nWeaker models produce more diverse (and thus more frequently disagreeing) outputs but extract worse constraints (precision 0.49 for 7B vs.\\ 0.51 for 72B).\nStronger models extract marginally better constraints but produce insufficient diversity to exercise them.\nThis tradeoff is structural: it arises from the same capability that determines both answer consistency and constraint quality.\n\n\\paragraph{Relationship to published systems.}\nSystems like DyLoS, Aristotle, FoVer, and LogicAgent achieve gains on benchmarks overlapping with ours.\nThe key distinction is architectural: these systems employ trained verifiers, external oracles, logic-complete decomposition, or multi-paradigm solver selection.\nOur finding characterizes the specific failure mode of \\emph{same-model self-extraction} pipelines, not symbolic reasoning broadly.\nThe capability trap may be breakable by decoupling the extraction and reasoning models, as these systems implicitly do.\n\n\\paragraph{Reasoning models bypass the need entirely.}\nQwQ-32B, as a full reasoning model, achieves $C_0=2.6\\%$, making \\sica{} structurally degenerate.\nThis is consistent with the test-time compute scaling paradigm \\citep{snell2025scaling,deepseekr1}: models that invest compute in extended chains achieve consistency through deliberation rather than aggregation.\nFor reasoning models, the question of symbolic aggregation is moot.\n\n\\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}\nPractitioners considering symbolic aggregation over self-extracted constraints should:\n(1) Compute $C_0$ from a small pilot ($n \\geq 30$, $K=12$). If $C_0 < 5\\%$, the method will degenerate to SC.\n(2) Even if $C_0 > 20\\%$, do not expect gains without evidence that the extraction model produces discriminative constraints (precision $\\gg 0.50$).\n(3) Consider the $\\sim$2$\\times$ overhead: SC achieves the same accuracy at half the cost.\n\n% ============================================================\n% 6. CONCLUSION\n% ============================================================\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe presented a systematic evaluation of symbolic constraint aggregation via self-extracted FOL constraints (SICA) across 3 reasoning domains, 5 model families, and 18 experimental conditions.\nOur central finding is a \\emph{capability trap}: self-extracted constraints achieve chance-level discriminative precision, causing MAX-SAT to degenerate to counting and providing no improvement over simple majority voting.\nWe validated this through constraint ablation (MAX-SAT $\\equiv$ count-only $\\equiv$ random-weight), per-problem precision analysis ($n=307$, mean precision $= 0.50$), and cross-condition C0 analysis ($r = 0.05$ between diversity and gain).\nThe multi-candidate rate $C_0$ provides a zero-cost diagnostic for practitioners: it reliably predicts when symbolic aggregation cannot help, potentially saving significant inference overhead ($\\sim$2$\\times$ cost).\n\n\\paragraph{Limitations.}\nOur study is scoped to same-model self-extraction pipelines. Systems using trained verifiers, external oracles, or cross-model extraction may not share this limitation.\nWe test one MAX-SAT formulation; alternative symbolic aggregation strategies (e.g., SAT, SMT, answer set programming) could yield different results.\nGSM8K and ARC-Challenge evaluations use smaller samples ($n \\leq 200$); powered replications on these domains would strengthen conclusions.\n\n% ============================================================\n% REFERENCES\n% FOL 标注，这个实验完全可行。\n\n## Should-Fix 问题（影响评分但不一票否决）\n\n**W1** [warning] Constraint extraction prompt 和示例完全缺失\n- 具体位置：Section 3, Stage 2 (L125-127)\n- 问题：论文只说 \"prompt the same LLM to extract FOL constraints\"，但 prompt 模板、few-shot 示例、输出格式要求都没有。这是方法论的核心环节。\n- 建议：在 Appendix 提供完整 prompt 模板和至少 2 个 extraction 示例（含输入 trace 和输出 constraints）。\n\n**W2** [warning] Temperature τ 未指定\n- 具体位置：Section 3, Stage 1 (L120-121)\n- 问题：τ 是控制 trace diversity 的关键超参，直接影响 C0 值。论文只说 \"τ > 0\" 但从未给出具体值。\n- 建议：报告所有实验使用的 τ 值。如果不同实验用了不同 τ，需要说明。\n\n**W3** [warning] Table 1 中 LLaMA-8B 两行缺少绝对 accuracy\n- 具体位置：Table 1, LLaMA-3.1-8B 行\n- 问题：SICA Acc 和 SC Acc 列显示 \"--\"，仅报告 Δ。读者无法判断绝对性能水平（如果 base accuracy 很低，+2pp 的意义不同于 base 很高时的 +2pp）。\n- 建议：补全所有条件的绝对 accuracy。\n\n**W4** [warning] Confidence intervals 未在 Table 1 中展示\n- 具体位置：Section 4.1 Metrics paragraph 提到 \"95% bootstrap confidence intervals for powered tests\"，但 Table 1 没有 CI 列\n- 问题：CI 仅在正文中为 LLaMA-8B 两个条件提及。对于 negative result paper，CI 比 p-value 更能传达信息（CI 宽度直接展示了实验对效应量的约束力）。\n- 建议：在 Table 1 中为所有 n≥200 条件加 CI 列。\n\n**W5** [warning] Constraint precision 分析仅基于 Qwen-14B 一个模型\n- 具体位置：Section 4.4 (L267-283)\n- 问题：per-problem constraint precision 分析（n=307, mean=0.50）仅来自 Qwen-14B。论文将此泛化为 \"the capability trap\" 的结构性解释，但未在其他模型上验证 precision 分布。Appendix D 的 scaling 表给出 Qwen-7B precision=0.49, 72B=0.51，但都是 n=60 pilots。\n- 建议：至少在 LLaMA-8B（有 n=204 和 n=200 的 \"contribution\"。或者，如果能展示 C0 在 early stopping 中的实际节省（如跳过 constraint extraction 的 cost saving），则更有说服力。\n\n**W7** [warning] 全文零 figure\n- 具体位置：全文 11 页\n- 问题：作为一篇实证研究论文，没有任何 figure 篇。不过对于 top venue，补充 R2 列出的那几篇确实必要。\n\n---\n\n### 回应 N3: Capability Trap 概念独立贡献\n\n[AGREE] R2-N3（部分同意）: R2 正确指出四个子组件单独来看都不算新洞察。capability trap 的贡献主要在于将这些观察整合到一个诊断框架中，并提供了定量验证。\n\n但我要指出：R2 认为\"组合增量主要是量化（阈值数字），但样本量较小（n=30-60）\"——这与我的 N2 观点一致。论文最大的问题不是 novelty 不足，而是 **underpowered experiments 导致量化结论不可靠**。如果量化是核心贡献，那量化的统计基础必须扎实，但目前 8/11 条件 n≤60，这让 capability trap 的精确边界条件（如 precision>0.6 阈值、~31% 等数字）缺乏可信的统计支撑。\n\n---\n\n### 回应 W1: Oracle 实验仅限 FOLIO\n\n[REBUT] R2-W1: **论文中不存在 oracle 实验。** 我在审稿前用 grep 逐一核实了 paper.tex 中 \"oracle\"、\"gold\"、\"8.82\"、\"upper bound\" 的所有出现位置：\n\n- \"oracle\" 仅出现在 L54、L411、L438，全部是 \"external oracles\" 语境（指其他系统架构），不是本文自己的实验\n- \"gold\" 仅出现在 L175 \"gold answer\"（评估标准定义），不是 gold FOL constraints\n- \"+8.82\" 不出现在论文任何位置\n- 论文全文 700 行 LaTeX，无任何 oracle experiment section、oracle table、或 gold FOL annotation 实验\n\n这与我在 Round 1 审稿中提出的 **N6 (Missing oracle/upper-bound experiment)** 完全一致：论文声称 capability trap 的根源是 self-extracted constraints 质量不足，但未通过 oracle control 验证 \"好的 constraints 是否真能帮助 MAX-SAT 超越 SC\"。R2 在 W1 中讨论 oracle 实验 \"仅限 FOLIO\" 的泛化性问题，但前提（oracle 实验存在）不成立。\n\n**这一分歧的可能原因**：Director 原始任务描述的\"论文摘要\"中包含 \"Oracle experiment: Gold FOL on FOLIO n=204 → +8.82pp (p<0.001)\" 条目，但该数据不在实际提交的论文 PDF/LaTeX 中。R2 可能基于 Director 摘要而非论文本身做出了判断。\n\n**结论**：oracle 实验缺失是 **must-fix 问题（我的 N6）**，不是 \"仅限一个 domain 的 warning（R2 的 W1）\"。这个问题的严重程度应该上调。\n\n---\n\n### 回应 W2: Self-limitation 导致定位尴尬\n\n[AGREE] R2-W2（部分同意）: 论文确实存在 \"自设限制 → 发现方法不 work → 建议用别的方法\" 的循环论证风险。最终 practical recommendation（Section 5 L421-424）的第三条 \"Consider the ~2× overhead: SC achieves the same accuracy at half the cost\" 本质上是说 \"别用我们研究的方法\"。\n\n但我不认为这完全削弱论文价值。Negative result paper 的意义在于 \"characterizing WHY something doesn't work\"，而非仅说 \"it doesn't work\"。论文的 constraint ablation（Table 2）和 per-problem precision analysis（Section 4.4）确实提供了机制层面的解释。问题是这个解释的深度是否足够 top venue——如果补上 oracle experiment 和 powered experiments，论文的定位会从 \"it doesn't work\" 升级为 \"it doesn't work because X, and fixing X makes it work\"，这是显著更强的贡献。\n\n---\n\n### 回应 W3: ~31% 统计量的代表性\n\n[AGREE] R2-W3: 同意。这与我的 N2（underpowered experiments）和 N3（18 conditions 无法验证）高度相关。~31% 这个数字来源于特定的 model×domain 组合，其代表性受限于有限的实验覆盖。论文将其作为一般性结论呈现（Abstract L38: \"~31% of multi-candidate problems meet this threshold\"——但这个 31% 实际上在论文正文中未出现，可能来自 Director 摘要而非论文本身），存在 overgeneralization 风险。\n\n---\n\n### 回应 R2 总体评分和\"workshop paper\"建议\n\n部分同意。R2 给出 3/6 (Weak Reject) 并建议 workshop paper。我给出 2.5/5 ARR scale (Borderline Findings)。我们的核心判断一致：**论文当前形态不足以达到 main conference 录用标准**。\n\n关键分歧在于主要原因的归因：\n- R2 侧重 **novelty 不足**（与 Huang et al. 重叠、概念非新）\n- 我侧重 **soundness 不足**（underpowered experiments、method 描述缺失、内部矛盾）\n\n我认为两者是独立的、可叠加的问题。即使 novelty 问题通过更好的 positioning 和 related work 覆盖部分缓解，soundness 问题仍然独立存在（反之亦然）。综合两位 reviewer 的意见，论文需要同时解决 novelty positioning 和 experimental rigor 才可能达到 Findings 水平。\n",
  "reviewer_id": "1",
  "project": "symb_invariant_consensus"
}
